sentences: A man stands on a rocky summit, looking out over an endless sea of fog.
The German Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich made this picture around 1818, and it now hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle.
Friedrich often painted figures from behind, a device known in German as the Rückenfigur, and this is perhaps its most famous example.
Because we cannot see his expression, we naturally step into his place and look at the view with him.
He stands at the exact centre of the canvas, wrapped in a dark green overcoat, gripping a walking stick in his right hand, one foot planted on a higher rock.
His hair, caught in the wind, tells us how sharp the air is up here.
Follow the ridgelines on both sides, and you will find the slopes from left and right converging on him.
So however wide the view, the eye keeps returning to this one figure.
He is both the centre of the landscape and its key.
The large mountain in the left background is thought to be the Rosenberg or the Kaltenberg.
The group of rocks rising from the mist in front of it is identified as the Gamrig, near Rathen.
The fog makes every distance feel even more remote.
Far off to the right, the flat-topped rock is the Zirkelstein.
All of these come from real places in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains, which stretch across Saxony and Bohemia, though you could never see them together like this from one spot.
Friedrich sketched these sites in the field and then combined them in the studio into one imagined panorama.
He wrote that mist makes things appear larger and more sublime, elevating the imagination.
The dark rocks beneath the man's feet belong to the Kaiserkrone.
The rough, heavy stone in front and the pale, soft fog beyond create a strong contrast that gives the picture its depth.
This rock becomes the threshold between us and the fog.
It is perhaps the clearest image of the sublime, the awe and fear before overwhelming nature that lay at the heart of Romanticism.
The figure is small, but the world before him has no visible end.
No one knows who this man is.
Some see a self-portrait, and some scholars read a political message in his clothing.
The painting entered the Hamburger Kunsthalle in 1970.
Friedrich wrote that the artist should paint not only what he has in front of him but also what he sees inside himself.
Standing in the wanderer's place and gazing down into the fog, what do you see within yourself?
